title.en: The Plat-Eye of the Georgetown Coast

region.en: Pawley's Island, Georgetown coast, South Carolina, USA
region.zh: 美國南卡羅來納喬治敦海岸保利島

texts.period: Gullah folk-belief; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Ambrose E. Gonzales, 'The Black Border: Gullah Stories of the Carolina Coast' (1922), tale 'The Plat-Eye' (Jane the cook's night-walk)

summary.en: A bogey peculiar to the Georgetown coast: plat-eyes appear to old and young of both sexes — sometimes as a small dog or other animal, sometimes floating like wraiths along the marshes, sometimes stooping like low-hung clouds to envelop the victim. Most often they come as a familiar animal glaring with eyes of fire, spring upon him, frighten him into rigidity, and just as he expects his vitals to be torn out, the apparition vanishes; the negroes dread the visitations as werewolves were feared in Europe not so long ago — and old Jane, the many-times-widowed cook, walks her nights on permanent jumpiness, seeing potential plat-eyes in every stray calf, raccoon, bouncing rabbit, and even the ghostly sandcrabs drifting along the beaches like windblown foam.
summary.zh: 喬治敦海岸特有的妖怪：『板眼』對男女老少都會現形——時而化為小狗或別的獸，時而如幽靈般漂浮於沼澤小徑，時而低垂如雲、將人裹住。最常見的是化作熟悉的動物、以火眼瞪視、撲向行人，令其僵立；正當他以為五臟要被掏出之際，妖物倏忽消失。當地人畏之如歐洲人昔時畏狼人；屢屢喪夫的廚娘簡，夜行時神經緊繃——離群的小牛、浣熊、竄起的兔子、連沙灘上隨風飄移的幽靈沙蟹，在她眼裡都是潛伏的板眼。

sensitivity.note: Gullah bogey-tale from Gonzales's coastal South Carolina collection; dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: All low-country negroes believe more or less in 'sperrits', 'haants' and other mysterious appearances, but the plat-eye, peculiar to the Georgetown coast, is the weirdest and most fearsome that vexes the roaming negroes at night. Plat-eyes appear to old and young of both sexes, sometimes in the form of a small dog or other animal, while at other times they may float like wraiths along the marshes or unfrequented paths, or stoop like low-hung clouds and envelop the victim.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, The Black Border, 'The Plat-Eye' (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Most frequently, however, the plat-eye appears in the form of some familiar animal which, glaring at the beholder with eyes of fire, springs upon him, frightening him into rigidity — and, just as he expects his vitals to be torn out, the apparition vanishes, and the trembling negro hurries on his way. The belief has been expressed that in some instances the negroes to whom plat-eyes appear have fallen asleep as they walked, and, dreaming of these terrors, awakened to find them gone. In whatsoever form they come, however, the negroes dread the visitations as werewolves were feared in Europe not so long ago.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Plat-Eye', middle (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Old Jane, the cook at the Pawley's Island summer hotel — the many-times-widowed woman who had saved the life of Esau the fisherman by drenching him with horse liniment, wedded him to save herself the reproach of old-maidenhood, and chased him away the morning after — was a fervent and fearful believer in plat-eyes. Whenever and wherever she went her ways at night, she was on the lookout for them, and the expectation of their momentary appearance kept her nerves in a pleasant state of jumpiness: a stray calf at the edge of the clearing, a raccoon ambling along a woodland path, a sudden rabbit bouncing up before her, the horned owl that lifted her wayward fowls from their runaway roost on the ridge-pole of her cabin — even the ghostly sandcrabs that drifted along the beaches at night as lightly as windblown foam — were all potential plat-eyes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Plat-Eye', ending (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Old Harrison and Ben: 'God Held My Hand'
title.zh: 老哈里森與本恩：『是上帝按住了我的手』

region.zh: 美國南卡羅來納庫珀河一帶

texts.period: Post-emancipation Gullah life; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Ambrose E. Gonzales, 'The Black Border' (1922), tale 'Old Harrison' (Ben's testimony of the beating)

summary.en: Ben, a rascal twice over — six or seven wives put away and taken back at his pleasure, always under suspicion when a calf or shoat went missing — undertook to discipline his step-daughter-in-law, an Amazon who took two or three blows of the hickory and then turned on him and mauled him almost into unconsciousness. Patched up, he loved to tell the story with unction: 'God bin wid me dat day... me 'membuh de time when I could-uh box her and kick her... but God tell me fuh peaceubble, en' spayre de 'ooman life... ef I had a kick dat 'ooman 'e would-uh dead' — and when he looks upon the dead woman in his mind, he thanks God every day for holding his hand.
summary.zh: 劣跡斑斑的本恩——七八任妻子隨心聚散、失牛失豬總被懷疑——竟要『管教』力大如亞馬遜的繼媳；胡桃棍落下兩三記，那女子轉身反擊，幾乎將他打昏。傷癒之後他逢人便講，油然自得：『那天上帝與我同在……想當年我拳腳並施她早沒命了……可上帝命我息怒、饒她性命……每當我腦中浮現那具女屍，我就天天感謝上帝按住了我的手。』

sensitivity.note: Gullah anecdote-frame tale with dark domestic-violence content, transcribed by Gonzales from coastal tellers; presented as documentary folk narrative. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: Ben had been partial to wives all his life, having been more or less affiliated with six or seven, whom he put away and took back again with no more ceremony than his change of mind. Unruly and insubordinate as a slave, he became stronger with freedom, and was regarded as a rascal by whites and blacks: when a calf or a shoat was missed in the community, Ben was not infrequently suspected of having shared the meat, either as a participant in the slaughter or as a welcomed guest at the banqueting board of the thief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, The Black Border, 'Old Harrison' (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of Ben's wives had achieved a son by a former husband, and this stepson had acquired a wife — a husky, corn-fed wench, an Amazon in strength and fierceness. Soon after her marriage old Ben, a rough-talking, brutal fellow who tyrannized over the women of his entourage, undertook to discipline this step-daughter-in-law with physical chastisement; cutting a hickory, he proceeded to manhandle her as he had been accustomed to use his wives. She accepted two or three blows, and then turned upon him so swiftly that he was swept off his feet and mauled almost into unconsciousness.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Old Harrison', middle (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: After he had been patched up and rehabilitated, and the first bitterness of defeat had worn off, he really liked to tell the story, laying the unction to his soul that only his Christian spirit had stayed his hand and saved the life of the virago: 'General, let me tell you the truth — God was with me that day. All my life I have been a strong man; no man ever outdid me at work or at fighting, and I have been used to lick women and things all my life... So I cut one stick and I grabbed her by the sleeve and began to lick her. General, the woman turned on me and boxed me like him dull man. Blood was in my eye! I remember the time when I could-uh box her and kick her a little two-one-time, and if I ever had let the foot follow the hand, I would-uh killed her dead. But God held my hand and my foot both; God told me to be peaceable and spare the woman's life. I don't want no woman's life upon my hand. Do you not know, sir, if I had kicked that woman she would-uh dead? God took care of old Ben that day. That woman thinks she licked me, General — but do you not know she ought to thank God for sparing her? If I had not had religion, that woman's corpse would have gone to Jacksonboro in one ox-cart! When I look upon the dead woman in my mind, I thank God every day for holding my hand!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Old Harrison', ending (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come: Minzacter's Divorce
title.zh: 等候新郎到來：明扎克特的離婚案

region.zh: 美國南卡羅來納下游地區

texts.period: Post-emancipation Gullah life; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Ambrose E. Gonzales, 'The Black Border' (1922), tale 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come' (Minzacter Singleton's crop, crow, and courtroom)

summary.en: Plowing his one-third of the corn, Minzacter Singleton addresses the circling crow as the tithe-taking friar of the field — 'take care buzzut don't dance at your funeral this same berry fall!' — and meets at the row's end the constable and a brown woman who has come with a marriage certificate and the Goose Creek pastor to haul him to the Trial Justice. His answers to the court — 'I nebbuh see you sence I bawn' — carry the tale to its comic verdict, the crow of the field presiding over the whole church-wedding muddle.
summary.zh: 明扎克特犁著自己那三分之一的玉米田，把盤旋的烏鴉斥為田間什一稅的托缽僧——『當心今秋烏鴉不敢在你的葬禮上起舞！』——壟頭卻站著警吏與一位持結婚證書、偕牧師而來的棕衣婦人，要拖他去見初審法官。他一句『我打娘胎起就沒見過你』的庭答，把這樁教堂婚事鬧成滑稽的判決；田裡的烏鴉，正是這場混亂的見證者。

sensitivity.note: Gullah comic anecdote-frame tale. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase.

passages.text: On a hot June day a year or two ago, a tall, pumpkin-colored negro was leisurely plowing an unambitious mule in a cornfield in Lower Carolina. Minzacter Singleton was his euphonious name, and he was about fifty-five years of age. As he passed up and down the furrows he whistled cheerily, for the brown earth that curled away in long waves from his plowshare was mellow and rich, and the bourgeoning corn around him — a grand industrial army uniformed in blue-green, epauletted with crimson silk and plumed with cream-white tassels — was full of promise for the autumn.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come' (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: High up in the blue, a crow flew slowly over the field, twisting his head from side to side while he critically inspected the work in progress; and, finding that it was good, croaked out an occasional 'ckwarrow, ckwarrow.' As the friar of the middle ages — the prototype of this black-robed fellow — unctuously took from the fields of his flock a tithe of the garnered store, so, when the blades should be stripped away and September suns harden the grain, would this 'sukkus preechuh' claim the reward of his interest in and inspection of the growing crop. As the ominous shadow passed between him and the sun, Minzacter, looking up, said: 'Never mind, brother! Take care buzzut doesn't dance at your funeral this same berry fall! You are smart enough to know when a man has a gun in his hand, but your education cannot specify when the shelled corn has pizen in it. You fly high in the elements today — take care you don't flew low before Christmas come!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come', middle (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: Upon reaching the end of his row, Minzacter found awaiting him the burly black constable of a neighboring Trial Justice, accompanied by a middle-aged brown woman: 'Mister Singleton, I thought you was a gentleman, but I come to find out you cannot specify as a gentleman, because you run away and left me over to Goose Creek, and gone and married Paul Jenkins's gramma just because she got four cow and I have not got no cow. You run away and left your lawfully lady, and I come to take you to the Trial Justice to throw you in Walterboro jail.' With apparent nonchalance Minzacter said: 'Go away, gal! Who you call husbun'? I never see you since I was bawn. I has got no time for holding composition with every which-and-why woman that comes along the road. This corn has got to lay by.' Julia Singleton, the ecru claimant, left him with the threat that she would go home and fetch the marriage stipulation to prove that Minzacter was her lawful husband — and sure enough, on the day set for the preliminary examination, she appeared with not only the marriage certificate, but accompanied by her brother and the Rev. Sancho Middleton, the Goose Creek locus-pastor, who was alleged to have performed the ceremony.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'Waiting Till the Bridegrooms Come', ending (1922); not verbatim.

title.en: The Lion Killer: Fat Negroes and Escaped Lions

region.en: Pon Pon district, South Carolina, USA
region.zh: 美國南卡羅來納蓬蓬區

texts.period: Post-emancipation Gullah tale; recorded early 20th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Ambrose E. Gonzales, 'The Black Border' (1922), tale 'The Lion Killer' (Joe's account of the escaped lion on the Cumbee)

summary.en: When the lion escaped from Orangeburg, he ran spang to the Sawlketchuh swamp and never stopped till he got to Lewisburg — for Massa's negroes are fat, fat as a soul, and the lion can smell a fat negro farther than a lean one. Locked in their houses all night with fires built so he cannot come down the chimney, the terrified people pray and bargain with the Lord — one promises never to steal Massa's rice again if He only takes the lion's jaw off him, every one confessing some light sin they are willing to throw away if their lives are spared — while the heavy sins they hold like a sheep holds a mule's tail till Gabriel blows his horn.
summary.zh: 獅子從奧蘭治堡逃出，直奔索爾凱丘沼澤，一路不停直到劉易斯堡——因為主人家的黑奴胖得很，獅子嗅胖奴比嗅瘦奴遠得多。眾人整夜閉戶、生火防它從煙囪下來，嚇得紛紛禱告交易——一個許諾只要上帝把獅口挪開便永不偷主人家的米，人人供認些『輕罪』願意拋卻換命——而『重罪』嘛，且像羊叼驢尾般握著，直等到加百列吹號、上帝親手取走。

sensitivity.note: Gullah humorous horror-tale from Gonzales's collection. Dialect rendered to standard English in paraphrase; the period term 'fat negroes' is the teller's own framing, noted as such.

passages.text: When the lion got away out of the circus, he went spang from Orangeburg to the Sawlketchuh swamp and never stopped till he got to Lewisburg. Why should he stop at Lewisburg? Do you not know, sir, that Massa's negroes are fat — fat as a soul! The lion has sense enough to know a fat negro when he sees him, and he can smell a fat negro farther than he can smell a lean one — and Massa makes his negroes fat on heavier crops of rice and lettuce and things than all the other negroes on the Cumbee river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, The Black Border, 'The Lion Killer' (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: As soon as the lion got to Lewisburg he stopped, knowing his dinner was there, and his mouth began to run water. By and by in the nighttime his voice rolled in Massa's pineland, and all the negroes were terrified like a chicken terrified when the hawk's wing throws its shadow over them! They were afraid till they were foolish; they locked themselves in their houses all night, and, although it was the dead summertime, they made fires to burn so the lion could not come down the chimney.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Lion Killer', middle (1922); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the lion could get no negroes to eat because they were all locked up, he went into the wood and met a cow and killed her for his dinner; and after he had eaten the three cows — 'Three cows! How can he eat three cows when he only killed one?' — 'He can eat them, sir; I don't know if he ate them dead. You ever see a lion? What does a Pon Pon negro know about a lion?' — he went back to the negro-house yard to see if he could get a chance to eat a negro. He walked up and down, thrashed his tail, gnashed his teeth, and hollered like a jackass and an alligator and a bull all at one time! You could hear the negroes in their houses praying: every one of them promised Jesus to follow His word if He only spared their lives — one told Him that if He took the lion's jaw off him, he would never steal Massa's rice again — and every one told the Lord about some of those light sins which they were willing to throw away if their lives were spared. Light sins! Why did they not promise to throw away their heavy sins? 'No, man; they are not going to throw away their heavy sins — I don't know if the lion would crack their bones. In slavery time a negro begged his massa's pardon for stealing his fowl when he got caught, but when he killed a cow he never cracked his teeth... No, man; you hold your heavy sin like a sheep holds a mule's tail, till Gabriel blow his horn and the Lord take it off!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Gonzales, 'The Lion Killer', ending (1922); not verbatim.
